text: This capstone starts the same way most real cloud work does -- not as a fully scoped project, but as one sentence from one stakeholder.

You're Theo Bryant, a new Cloud Engineer at Driftwood Outdoor Apparel. The product-catalog app runs on one aging on-prem server with no real monitoring. Your IT Manager, Priya Suresh, asks you to migrate the catalog app to Azure before an upcoming product launch -- the images, and the server itself. Three things in that ask are each hiding a real question. The images -- where do they actually live today? The server -- recreate exactly, or also fix what was never right? And before launch -- what's the actual date, and how much buffer is there to catch problems?

None of those are hard questions. They're just questions nobody's answered yet. A short follow-up conversation gets you three concrete answers: the workload, the deadline, and the definition of done -- before you touch the Azure Portal or CLI.

After that conversation, the vague ask becomes something specific: migrate the product-catalog app's static product images and its application server from on-prem to Azure, with basic monitoring in place, fully validated at least one week before the product launch. That's now a sentence you could hand to a teammate and get the same understanding back.

Scoping also means noticing what you don't know yet, without guessing early. Which specific Azure services fit best is next lesson's job. Whether the app itself needs to change isn't assumed -- same app, new home, until you learn otherwise. And Priya asked about one app on one deadline, not a company-wide cloud strategy.
With the ask written down, next lesson turns it into a concrete scope -- exactly what's in this first migration, and just as importantly, what's deliberately left out.
